newsitem.title: USA: ABC told to pay $5.5 million in Food Lion case.
newsitem.headline: ABC told to pay $5.5 million in Food Lion case.

text.p: A federal jury on Wednesday ordered ABC television to pay Food Lion Inc. $5.5 million in punitive damages as a result of the network's undercover investigation of the supermarket chain.
The panel deliberated more than 30 hours over six days before reaching the decision, which also ordered two producers for ABC's newsmagazine "PrimeTime Live" to pay damages totalling $45,750.
Executives of ABC, a subsidiary of Walt Disney Co., said they would appeal the jury award.

Food Lion, based in Salisbury, N.C., sued ABC over a 1992 "PrimeTime Live" report that charged that Food Lion sold spoiled meat and other outdated merchandise and did not use sanitary food handling practices.
"The verdict of the North Carolina jury should trouble every American -- especially every journalist," ABC News President Roone Arledge said in a statement.
He said that lawyers for Food Lion were successful in convincing the jury to "punish" ABC simply for using undercover investigative techniques.
Food Lion never challenged the truthfulness of the 1992 broadcast but sued ABC for fraud for having two journalists break the law to get jobs with Food Lion.

The jury found last month that ABC committed fraud, trespass and breach of loyalty when two of its television journalists obtained jobs with Food Lion stores, one as a meat handler and the other as a deli clerk.
The panel earlier had awarded the grocer some $1,400 in actual damages.

"After finding that the use of those undercover techniques caused Food Lion only token damages, the jury has now awarded Food Lion punitive damages of 4,000 times that amount. That result in unconscionable," Arledge said in his statement.
The jury of six men and six women also ordered "PrimeTime Live" Executive Producer Richard Kaplan to pay $35,000 and senior producer Ira Rosen to pay $10,750.
Food Lion lawyers suggested during closing arguments that Kaplan and Rosen be assessed $50,000 each in punitive damages.

The jury did not assess damages against ABC journalists Lynne Dale and Susan Barnett, who worked undercover at Food Lion stores. They had worked with cameras hidden in their hair and recorders under their smocks.

They filmed spoiling deli products, meat cutters and machines that were not properly cleaned, rat-gnawed cheese and other unsanitary conditions for the Nov. 5, 1992, broadcast that came during a "rating sweeps" period.

Food Lion lawyers last week urged the jury to order ABC to pay "very large" damages for the program -- so large that the network and others would be deterred from conducting future hidden-camera reports that break the law in the process.
Food Lion's stock gained 6.25 cents to $9.125 in afternoon trading on the Nasdaq market.
Shares of Walt Disney, which acquired ABC television as part of its 1995 merger with Capitalcities/ABC Inc., gained 12.5 cents to $69.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
